grammar.explanation: Attach 처럼 directly to a noun to say something is done in the same way as that noun, or resembles it. The phrase works like an adverb in the sentence. It can also follow ~에서 or a ~는 것 clause (~는 것처럼) to compare whole actions.

examples.en: Our son is tall like his dad.
Don’t laugh like an idiot.
That child talks like an adult.

examples.ko: 저는 한국 사람이 하는 것처럼 김치를 만들었어요.
examples.en: I made kimchi the way Koreans do.

grammar.explanation: Put a clause in its modifier form (~는/~(으)ㄴ/~(으)ㄹ) before 듯(이) to mean “as if”. The speaker is guessing what the situation seemed to be, and the two clauses are directly related. The 이 can be dropped with no change in meaning.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 아무것도 모르는 듯이 웃었어요.
examples.en: He laughed as if he knew nothing.

examples.ko: 동생이 배가 고픈 듯이 밥을 빨리 먹었어요.
examples.en: My sibling ate fast as if he was hungry.

examples.ko: 친구가 나를 못 본 듯이 그냥 지나갔어요.
examples.en: My friend walked right past as if he hadn’t seen me.

grammar.explanation: Adding 듯이 straight onto a verb or adjective stem builds a vivid metaphor, often an exaggerated image, that matches the feeling of the main clause. There is no guessing here, and the two clauses are not logically connected. It mostly shows up in writing such as novels.

examples.en: The rain came down as if a waterfall were pouring.
He drank alcohol like it was water.
Time flew by like an arrow.

grammar.explanation: Put 듯하다 after a modifier clause at the end of a sentence to say “it seems that…”. It sounds a bit softer and more formal than ~는 것 같다.

examples.en: It seems to be raining outside.
That person seems to have a lot of experience.
The child seems tired.

grammar.explanation: 마치 is an adverb near the start of a sentence that tells the listener a comparison is coming. It is usually paired with ~처럼, ~듯이 or 같다, much like 만약 goes with ~(으)면.

examples.en: She is as pretty as an actress.

examples.ko: 그는 마치 아무 일도 없었던 듯이 웃었어요.
examples.en: He smiled as if nothing had happened.
Today feels just like summer.

grammar.explanation: 유일하다 is an adjective, so 유일한 goes before a noun to mark it as the one and only thing with some quality. ~만 just limits the action to a noun, but 유일한 makes the noun stand out from all others. The noun is often also described by a ~는 clause, as in ~는 유일한 (noun).

examples.ko: 그 사람이 우리 반에서 유일한 외국인이에요.
examples.en: He is the only foreigner in our class.
This is the only photo I have.

examples.ko: 제가 매일 마시는 유일한 음료는 커피예요.
examples.en: The only drink I have every day is coffee.

grammar.explanation: Add ~게 to make the adverb 유일하게, usually placed before the describing verb or adjective. Use it instead of 유일한 when an adjective already describes the noun, because two stacked adjective modifiers sound awkward.

examples.ko: 제가 유일하게 할 수 있는 운동은 수영이에요.
examples.en: The only exercise I can do is swimming.

examples.ko: 동물원에서 유일하게 보고 싶은 동물은 코끼리예요.
examples.en: The only animal I want to see at the zoo is the elephant.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 우리 회사에서 유일하게 친절한 사람이에요.
examples.en: He is the only kind person at our company.

lessons.title: Lesson 69: Nothing but: 밖에 (~ㄹ/을 수밖에 없다)

grammar.explanation: The particle 밖에 (literally “outside of”) goes on a noun to stress that only that noun applies, and nothing else. The predicate must be negative (없다, 안, 못, 모르다), even though English uses a positive “only”. It is stronger than ~만 and is often used with numbers and counters.

examples.en: I only have 1,000 won in my wallet.
I can only speak a little Korean.
There is only one cabbage in the fridge.
He only cares about himself.

grammar.explanation: 밖에 is often put on an amount of time to stress how short it is, with a negative verb such as 안 걸리다.

examples.ko: 집에서 학교까지 십 분밖에 안 걸려요.
examples.en: It only takes ten minutes from home to school.
The homework only took an hour.

examples.ko: 그 영화는 한 번밖에 안 봤어요.
examples.en: I have only seen that movie once.

grammar.point: ~ㄹ/을 수밖에 없다 (have no choice but to)
grammar.explanation: Because 수 in ~ㄹ/을 수 없다 is a noun, 밖에 can attach to it. The result means the action is the only option left: “have no choice but to” or “can’t help but”.

examples.en: There was no bus, so I had no choice but to walk.

examples.ko: 내일이 마감일이라서 오늘 밤에 일할 수밖에 없어요.
examples.en: Tomorrow is the deadline, so I have no choice but to work tonight.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 너무 웃겨서 웃을 수밖에 없었어요.
examples.en: He was so funny I couldn’t help laughing.

vocab.en: to finish off, to wrap up

grammar.explanation: Like ~고, ~아/어(서) joins two actions in order, but it suggests the first action makes the second possible (for example, going somewhere and then doing something there). In this use 서 is optional.

examples.en: I went to school and met a friend.
I came home and slept.
I washed the apple and ate it.

grammar.explanation: ~아/어서 can show how, or by what means, the second action happens. In this use 서 cannot be dropped. 걸어서 집에 갔어요 can only mean “went home on foot”.

examples.en: I went home on foot.
My friend ran to school.
I saved up money and bought a car.

grammar.explanation: Two verbs joined with ~아/어 (no 서) form a combined verb such as 뛰어다니다, 달려오다 or 올려놓다. The result works like any normal verb.

examples.en: The kids are running around the park.
Mom came running to me.
I put the book on the desk.
Please let me know the time.

grammar.explanation: From 통하다, the form (noun)을/를 통해(서) means “through” or “by way of”. It can be a place you pass through, or the object, process or person you learn or hear something from.

examples.ko: 저는 친구를 통해서 그 소식을 들었어요.
examples.en: I heard the news through a friend.
Please go in through this door.

examples.ko: 저는 영화를 통해 한국 문화를 배웠어요.
examples.en: I learned about Korean culture through movies.

grammar.explanation: 서두르다 means “to hurry” (르 irregular → 서둘러). It often comes before another verb with ~아/어(서) to say that action was done in a rush.

examples.en: I was late, so I hurried out of the house.
I hurried and finished my homework.
Don’t rush.

vocab.en: to be early, to be premature

grammar.explanation: 포함하다 means “to include”, but at the end of a sentence the passive 포함되다 (with ~이/가 on the item) usually sounds more natural. It is often followed by ~어 있다.

examples.en: Tax is included in this price.
Is the gas bill included in the rent?
Breakfast is included.

grammar.explanation: Put 포함해(서) after a noun to mean “including (noun)”, then continue the sentence. ~(으)면 also works (포함하면, “if you include”).

examples.en: Five people came, including me.
I traveled for ten days, including the weekend.
How much is it if you include the fees?

grammar.explanation: To exclude something, use (noun)을/를 제외하고, which splits the sentence into two clauses, or 제외한 + noun, which describes the following noun. Use 제외하고 for times and places, or when another clause already describes the noun. Unlike 포함하다, 제외하다 is not normally used with ~아/어서.

examples.en: I work every day except Sunday.

examples.ko: 저를 제외한 모든 사람이 문신이 있어요.
examples.en: Everyone except me has a tattoo.
Everyone came except him.

grammar.explanation: In everyday speech, 빼다 (“to take out”) often replaces 제외하다. It is common when ordering food to ask for something to be left out, often dropping 을/를 or even 주세요.

examples.en: Please leave the ham out of the kimbap.
Without cucumber, please.
Everyone went except me.

grammar.explanation: 외 (外) means “outside”. Put 외에 after a noun, or use 그 외에 for something already mentioned, to talk about everything beyond it: “besides” or “other than”.

examples.en: Besides Korean, I also study Japanese.
Do you have any other questions besides that?
No one knows except this person.

grammar.explanation: Attach 만큼 to a noun to say something is done to the same level or extent as that noun: “as … as (noun)”. Unlike 처럼, which compares manner, 만큼 compares degree.

examples.en: My younger sibling is as tall as me.
That person sings as well as a singer.
I can’t eat as much as my older brother.

grammar.explanation: 만큼 can also be a noun described by a clause in the past, present or future (~ㄴ/는/ㄹ 만큼). Future-tense clauses often give exaggerated images, as in “so much I could die”. ~는 것만큼 can replace ~는 만큼, but not with the future tense.

examples.en: Eat as much as you want.
You get results in proportion to your effort.
I ate so much my stomach could burst.

grammar.explanation: 정도 means “degree”. Described by a clause (often future ~ㄹ 정도로), it shows the extent of something, much like 만큼. After a number or counter it means “about” or “roughly”.

examples.en: I’m so tired I could die.
I laughed so hard I cried.
It takes about two hours to Seoul.
About ten people came.

grammar.point: 어느 정도 / 얼마만큼 (to what extent / to some extent)
grammar.explanation: In a question, 어느 정도 or 얼마만큼 asks “how much” or “to what extent”. In a statement, 어느 정도 means “to some extent” or “fairly”.

examples.ko: 한국어를 어느 정도 할 수 있어요?
examples.en: How well can you speak Korean?
I understood to some extent.
How much do you love me?

grammar.explanation: Put 대신(에) after a noun to mean “instead of (noun)”. 에 is usually attached, but it can be dropped.

examples.en: I drank tea instead of coffee.
I went instead of my friend.
I ate bread instead of rice.

grammar.explanation: To replace one action with another, use verb stem + ~는 것 대신에 or ~는 대신에. They mean the same thing. Always use the present ~는 form, even when talking about the past or future.

examples.en: Instead of taking the bus, I walked.

examples.ko: 게임을 하는 것 대신에 공부를 했어요.
examples.en: Instead of playing games, I studied.

examples.ko: 영화를 보는 대신에 책을 읽을 거예요.
examples.en: Instead of watching a movie, I’ll read a book.

grammar.explanation: 차라리 adds the feeling that the speaker would prefer this option over another, usually less appealing one. It often saves you from spelling out “instead of …”.

examples.en: I’d rather walk than take a taxi.

examples.ko: 이렇게 기다릴 거면 차라리 집에 가요.
examples.en: If we’re going to wait like this, let’s just go home.
It’s better to just do it alone.

grammar.explanation: Just as ~지 말고 means “don’t do X, (do Y) instead” with verbs, 말고 can follow a noun directly: “not X, (but Y)”. It is very common in requests and choices.

examples.en: Not this one, give me that one.
I’ll have water, not coffee.
Let’s meet tomorrow instead of today.

lessons.title: Lesson 74: It doesn’t matter/ Regardless of (상관없다/상관없이)

vocab.en: to be dumped, to get kicked
to be faulty, to be poor

grammar.explanation: 상관 means “relation”, so 상관없다 says something is irrelevant. On its own it means “it doesn’t matter” or “I don’t mind”. With a clause, the irrelevant condition usually takes ~아/어도.

examples.en: It doesn’t matter if you’re late.
It doesn’t matter if it’s expensive.
It’s fine if you come tomorrow.

grammar.explanation: When the clause has a question word (when, where, who), ~아/어도 sounds unnatural. Use ~는지 or ~든지 before 상관없다 instead.

examples.en: It doesn’t matter where we go.
It doesn’t matter who you go with.
It doesn’t matter when we meet.

grammar.explanation: 상관없이 is the adverb form, meaning “regardless of”. The noun takes ~와/과, ~하고 or ~(이)랑. A full clause can come before it with ~는지.

examples.ko: 나이와 상관없이 누구나 가입할 수 있어요.
examples.en: Anyone can join regardless of age.
I exercise every day regardless of the weather.
You can apply regardless of nationality.

grammar.explanation: 불구하다 is used mid-sentence to mean “despite”. A noun takes ~에도 불구하고. A verb or adjective is first made into a noun with ~ㅁ/음 (past is possible: ~았/었음에도). It is used mostly in writing.

examples.en: Despite the rain, the game went on.

examples.ko: 부상에도 불구하고 그 선수는 끝까지 뛰었다.
examples.en: Despite the injury, the player ran to the end.
Despite studying hard, I failed the exam.

lessons.title: Lesson 75: I don’t care: 신경 안 쓰다

grammar.explanation: 신경 literally means “nerve”, but in daily speech it means attention or concern toward something. It is a noun, so a verb is needed to say you care: usually 쓰다.

examples.en: That person is very sensitive (high-strung).
I’m really bothered by the exam.
Don’t worry about it.

grammar.point: Noun에 (대해) 신경(을) 안 쓰다 (not care about)
grammar.explanation: The negative “I don’t care” is the most common use. Put ~에 대해 (or just ~에) on the thing you don’t care about. 을 on 신경 is often dropped in speech.

examples.ko: 저는 돈에 대해 신경 안 써요.
examples.en: I don’t care about money.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 옷에 신경을 안 써요.
examples.en: He doesn’t care about clothes.

examples.ko: 다른 사람의 말에 신경 쓰지 마세요.
examples.en: Don’t mind what other people say.

grammar.explanation: For a clause with a question word, use ~는지 (“I don’t care where/what…”), just as with 상관없다. ~아/어도 instead means “I don’t care even if…” and treats the question word as vague: it’s not even known whether the action happens.

examples.ko: 네가 어디에 가는지 신경 안 써.
examples.en: I don’t care where you go.
I don’t care even if it’s expensive.

examples.ko: 사람들이 뭐라고 하든지 신경 안 써요.
examples.en: I don’t care what people say.

grammar.explanation: The positive “I care” with 신경 쓰다 often sounds unnatural in statements. It is common in requests or commands telling someone to pay attention to something.

examples.en: Please take care of your health.

examples.ko: 손님이 오니까 청소에 신경 좀 써 주세요.
examples.en: Guests are coming, so please pay attention to the cleaning.

examples.ko: 운전할 때 신경을 많이 써야 해요.
examples.en: You need to pay close attention when driving.
